title: What training does OSHA require for forklift operators?
description: OSHA 1910.178(l) forklift operator training: formal, practical and workplace evaluation, three-year evaluations and refresher triggers, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires every powered industrial truck operator to be trained and evaluated before operating, under 29 CFR 1910.178(l). Training combines formal instruction, practical training and an evaluation of performance in the workplace, delivered by a person with the knowledge, training and experience to do so. Operators need a performance evaluation at least once every three years and refresher training after unsafe operation, incidents, a different truck type or workplace changes.
keyTakeaways: Online instruction alone does not satisfy the rule: paragraph (l)(2)(ii) requires formal instruction, practical training and evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace.
Initial training covers 13 truck-related topics, 9 workplace-related topics and the requirements of the standard, except topics the employer can show do not apply.
Each operator's performance must be evaluated at least once every three years, and refresher training is required after five listed triggers.
The employer certifies training and evaluation with the operator's name, training date, evaluation date and the identity of the trainer or evaluator.
Powered industrial trucks (29 CFR 1910.178) ranked seventh in OSHA's preliminary list of most cited standards for fiscal year 2026.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers, including manufacturing plants and warehouses, whose employees operate forklifts, tractors, platform lift trucks, motorized hand trucks or other specialized industrial trucks powered by electric motors or internal combustion engines
Trainees operating a truck under direct supervision during training
Persons who train and evaluate powered industrial truck operators

sections.heading: Which vehicles and employers does the forklift training rule cover?

blocks.text: The rule covers operators of powered industrial trucks in general industry. Paragraph (a)(1) of [29 CFR 1910.178](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.178) defines the scope as fork trucks, tractors, platform lift trucks, motorized hand trucks and other specialized industrial trucks powered by electric motors or internal combustion engines.

It does not apply to compressed air or nonflammable compressed gas operated trucks, farm vehicles, or vehicles intended primarily for earth moving or over-the-road hauling. In a manufacturing plant that usually means counterbalanced forklifts, reach trucks, order pickers, pallet jacks with a motor and tow tractors all fall inside the training requirement, while a delivery truck in the yard does not.

The operator training requirements in paragraph (l) were added by a final rule published on December 1, 1998 (63 FR 66270). Under paragraph (l)(7), any employee hired after December 1, 1999 must complete initial training and evaluation before being assigned to operate a truck.

sections.heading: How must forklift operator training be delivered?

blocks.text: Training must combine three elements. Paragraph (l)(2)(ii) requires "a combination of formal instruction (e.g., lecture, discussion, interactive computer learning, video tape, written material), practical training (demonstrations performed by the trainer and practical exercises performed by the trainee), and evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace."

Paragraph (l)(1)(i) frames the outcome: the employer must ensure each operator "is competent to operate a powered industrial truck safely, as demonstrated by the successful completion of the training and evaluation." This is a competence standard. A completion certificate from a classroom or online course shows only the first element.

items: **Who can train and evaluate:** persons who have the knowledge, training and experience to train powered industrial truck operators and evaluate their competence (paragraph (l)(2)(iii)). The rule does not require an external provider or a license.
**How trainees may drive:** only under direct supervision of such a person, and only where operation does not endanger the trainee or other employees (paragraph (l)(2)(i)).
**Where the evaluation happens:** in the workplace, which ties the evaluation to the employer's own trucks, loads, aisles and traffic.

sections.heading: What topics must initial forklift training cover?

blocks.text: Paragraph (l)(3) lists truck-related topics, workplace-related topics and the requirements of the section itself. An employer may omit a topic only if it can demonstrate the topic is not applicable to safe operation of the truck in its workplace.

blocks.caption: Initial training topics under 29 CFR 1910.178(l)(3)
head: Topic group
Topics listed in the rule
rows: Operating instructions, warnings and precautions for the truck types authorized; differences from an automobile; controls and instrumentation; engine or motor operation; steering and maneuvering; visibility including restrictions due to loading; fork and attachment adaptation, operation and limits; vehicle capacity; vehicle stability; any inspection and maintenance the operator will perform; refueling or battery charging; operating limitations; any other instructions in the operator's manual

Surface conditions; composition of loads and load stability; load manipulation, stacking and unstacking; pedestrian traffic; narrow aisles and restricted places; hazardous (classified) locations; ramps and sloped surfaces; closed environments where carbon monoxide or diesel exhaust can build up; other unique or hazardous environmental conditions

blocks.text: The workplace-related list is where generic courses fall short. A plant with a battery charging room, a mezzanine ramp and a busy assembly aisle needs those specific conditions covered and evaluated. Appendix A to the section gives non-mandatory guidance on truck stability; paragraph (l)(8) states it does not add to, alter or reduce the requirements.

sections.heading: How often must forklift operators be re-evaluated or retrained?

blocks.text: Every operator's performance must be evaluated at least once every three years under paragraph (l)(4)(iii). Separately, refresher training in relevant topics, including an evaluation of its effectiveness, is required under paragraph (l)(4)(ii) when:

items: The operator has been observed operating the vehicle in an unsafe manner.
The operator has been involved in an accident or near-miss incident.
The operator has received an evaluation revealing that the truck is not being operated safely.
The operator is assigned to drive a different type of truck.
A condition in the workplace changes in a manner that could affect safe operation of the truck.

blocks.text: The three-year evaluation is a minimum. It is not a three-year refresher course: the rule requires an evaluation of performance, and training only where the evaluation or another trigger shows it is needed. Paragraph (l)(5) also allows an employer to skip topics an operator was previously trained in, if that training suits the truck and conditions and the operator has been evaluated and found competent.

sections.heading: What must the forklift training certification contain?

blocks.text: Paragraph (l)(6) requires the employer to certify that each operator has been trained and evaluated. The certification must include the operator's name, the date of training, the date of evaluation, and the identity of the person or persons performing the training or evaluation. Wallet cards are common, but the rule asks for an employer certification, and a card from a previous employer does not replace evaluation in the new workplace.

sections.heading: How is the forklift rule enforced?

blocks.text: Federal OSHA and state plans enforce paragraph (l) through inspections, and it is cited often. OSHA's [preliminary top 10 for fiscal year 2026](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) places the general industry powered industrial trucks standard seventh across all industries. Maximum federal penalties assessed after January 15, 2026 are listed on [OSHA's penalties page](https://www.osha.gov/penalties) as $16,550 for a serious violation and $165,514 for a willful or repeated one.

An incident involving a truck is itself a refresher trigger, so investigators routinely ask for the operator's certification and evidence of refresher training after previous incidents. Keeping incident records and training records connected is the simplest defense, as described in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How should a plant design its forklift training program?

blocks.text: Design the program around authorization by truck type and location. Because a different truck type triggers refresher training, the authorization record should list each type an operator is cleared on, and the evaluation should be repeated per type.

items: Build a site-specific workplace module covering each item in (l)(3)(ii) that applies, with the plant's own aisles, ramps and charging areas.

Use a structured evaluation checklist so that evaluations are consistent across evaluators. The glossary entry on [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) explains how observed assessment differs from completion tracking.
Schedule three-year evaluations from each operator's last evaluation date, not from hire date, and connect near-miss reporting to the refresher workflow.
Record the qualifications of internal trainers and evaluators as evidence for (l)(2)(iii).

blocks.text: Related federal duties in the same plant often include [lockout/tagout training](/regulations/osha-lockout-tagout-training-requirements) for truck maintenance and [hazard communication training](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements) for battery electrolyte and fuels. For a view across standards, see [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each topic in paragraph (l)(3) to assessment points, separating knowledge checks from the observed workplace evaluation, and records authorization per truck type. Refresher triggers such as an incident or a new truck type open a targeted re-evaluation against the relevant points rather than a full course repeat.

faqs.q: Is forklift certification valid for three years?
faqs.a: The rule does not give certifications an expiry date. It requires a performance evaluation at least once every three years and refresher training whenever a listed trigger occurs. An operator involved in a near miss six months after evaluation needs refresher training then, not at the three-year mark.

faqs.q: Can forklift training be done entirely online?
faqs.a: No. Online modules can deliver the formal instruction element, but paragraph (l)(2)(ii) also requires practical training with demonstrations and trainee exercises, and an evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace by a qualified person.

faqs.q: Does a new hire with a forklift card from another employer need training?
faqs.a: The new employer must still certify the operator. Paragraph (l)(5) lets the employer skip topics already covered if that training suits the truck and conditions, but only after the operator has been evaluated and found competent. Workplace-specific topics and the evaluation cannot be inherited from another site.

faqs.q: Who can be a forklift trainer or evaluator?
faqs.a: Anyone with the knowledge, training and experience to train powered industrial truck operators and evaluate their competence. The rule sets no license or external accreditation. Employers should record why each internal trainer or evaluator meets that test.

factCheck.claim: 1910.178(a)(1) scope: fork trucks, tractors, platform lift trucks, motorized hand trucks and other specialized industrial trucks powered by electric motors or internal combustion engines; excludes compressed air or nonflammable compressed gas trucks, farm vehicles, earth moving and over-the-road vehicles.

1910.178(l)(2)(ii): training is a combination of formal instruction, practical training and evaluation of performance in the workplace; (l)(2)(iii) trainers and evaluators must have knowledge, training and experience; (l)(2)(i) trainees only under direct supervision.
1910.178(l)(3): 13 truck-related topics (A to M), 9 workplace-related topics (A to I), and the requirements of the section; topics may be omitted only where employer demonstrates non-applicability.
1910.178(l)(4)(ii) five refresher triggers and (l)(4)(iii) evaluation at least once every three years.

1910.178(l)(6): certification includes operator name, date of training, date of evaluation, identity of persons performing training or evaluation; (l)(5) avoidance of duplicative training; (l)(7) employees hired after December 1, 1999 trained before assignment; (l)(8) Appendix A non-mandatory.
Section amendment history includes 63 FR 66270, Dec. 1, 1998 (operator training rule).
